M0.p: A general heading for stories about judgments and decrees, meaning official rulings or commands that fix what will happen.

M1.p: A ruler or judge makes a decision that is foolish or makes no sense.

M2.p: A king makes cruel or inhuman decisions that harm his subjects.

M2.1.p: A king orders a man's sons sent to certain death, and then has the man himself murdered.

M4.p: A deity or god settles quarrels between different races or peoples.

M10.p: A general heading for judgments that cannot be changed or taken back once given.

M11.r: Kills himself. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 353; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
M11.p: A judge who has decreed that no armed person may enter a meeting is himself caught out when he forgets to leave his own sword outside, so the irrevocable judgment falls on him first.

M12.r: A centurion leads them to the emperor, who condemns all three to death: first because he has been sentenced; second for causing by his absence the conviction of his comrade; third for delay in the execution. Oesterley No. 140; Herbert III 208.
M12.p: A knight is condemned to death for murdering his comrade, and the sentence is carried out even after his innocence is shown: the comrade meets him on the way to the gallows.

M13.r: *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 226; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda.
M13.p: A ruler insists that the punishment for adultery, eyes put out, be applied to his own son. The son is found guilty, and the father finally compromises by blinding one of his own eyes and one of his son's.

M13.1.p: A ruler has his own son beheaded for rape.

M13.2.p: A military captain hangs his own son for disobeying an order not to enter an enemy city.

M13.3.p: A gardener who has been made king by a minister rules against him in a lawsuit and returns the disputed lands to the plaintiff.

M14.p: A king leaves laws that must be kept until his death. Years later he has his bones sent back to that land to show that he is dead and the people are free of his rule.

M20.p: A general heading for judgments that are short-sighted, meaning they fail to foresee their consequences.

M21.r: Type 510; BP II 47, III 305; *Cox Nos. 208—226; *Hartland FLJ IV 308; *Oesterley No. 273; Herbert III 201; India: *Thompson-Balys; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 183 No. 124.
M21.p: A king, flattered by his two elder daughters and angered by the seeming coolness of his youngest, who really loves him, banishes the youngest and favors the elder two.

M50.p: A general heading for judgments and decrees that do not fit the other categories.

M51.p: A decree requires that a hero marry only a virgin.

M55.p: A judge pardons the hero if he can produce the lady he has boasted about. The pardon depends on fulfilling the boast.

M56.p: A judge decides that a thief will be pardoned if he manages to steal the king's treasure without getting caught.

M90.p: A general heading for miscellaneous motifs about judgments and decrees, meaning formal rulings or verdicts, that do not fit elsewhere.

M91.r: *Ward II 638 No. 5, 651 No. 4, 668 No. 15, 682 No. 21, 704 No. 42, 722 No. 30 and passim; Irish: Beal XXI 315, O’Suilleabhain 41.
M91.p: The Virgin Mary overturns a ruling made by the church.

M92.r: Type 613; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 604b n. 31ff.; Irish: O’Suilleabhain 118, Beal XXI 335; India: *Thompson-Balys.
M92.p: A dispute or decision is left to be settled by whoever arrives first.

M93.p: A god grants a woman two sons: one is wise but ugly, and the other is a fool but handsome.

M100.r: *Penzer X 355 s.v. “vow”; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 659ff.; *Encyc. Rel. Ethics IX 430ff.; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 198ff.; Missouri French: Carrière; Jewish *Neuman.
M100.p: A general heading for motifs about vows and oaths, which are solemn promises made to gods or people.

M101.p: A general punishment that falls on someone who breaks a sworn oath.

M101.1.p: A person who swears falsely is forbidden to come near the altar.

M101.2.p: People are maimed as a result of having broken oaths.

M101.3.p: A broken oath is punished by death.

M101.3.1.p: The person who broke an oath dies from natural forces such as exposure, cold or drowning, as punishment.

M101.3.2.p: A man promises to sacrifice bangles if he is given a son. When he takes the bangles back, the son dies.

M101.4.p: A girl's hand withers as a punishment for breaking an oath.

M101.5.p: A broken oath costs the oath breaker any inheritance of the earth or of heaven.

M105.p: Oaths that are worded so they can be interpreted in two ways, so the swearer escapes the literal promise.

M106.p: Someone escapes revenge because of broken oaths.

M107.p: A vow is not fulfilled in this life but in the next existence.

M108.p: A general heading for people who break oaths.

M108.1.p: The Babylonians are said not to keep their oaths.

M110.p: A general motif about making solemn vows and oaths, a promise backed by an appeal to something sacred or binding.

M110.1.p: A person swears an oath even though they know the oath will have no value or force.

M110.2.p: An oath counts as binding only if it is sworn in the presence of ten people.

M110.3.p: A pious person swears an oath to protect themselves when they feel in danger of giving in to temptation.

M111.p: Oaths are sworn over the severed pieces of a horse, and the pieces are then buried.

M112.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 67; Brumer Deutsche Rechtsgeschichte I 258; Icelandic: *Boberg.
M112.p: An oath is sworn while holding or touching a ring.

M113.p: An oath is sworn on weapons or arms.

M113.1.r: Scottish: Campbell-McKay No. 20; Icelandic: Herrmann Saxo II 197; Jewish: Neuman.
M113.1.p: An oath is sworn on a sword.

M114.p: A person swears an oath by taking hold of or touching a sacred object.

M114.1.p: An oath is sworn on a sacred book.

M114.1.1.p: An oath is sworn by the Torah, the sacred Jewish scroll of law.

M114.2.p: An oath is sworn on a holy stone.

M114.3.p: Vows are taken on a holy pig.

M114.4.p: An oath is sworn on sacred relics, the preserved remains or objects of holy people.

M114.5.p: An oath is sworn on cow dung, which is considered sacred.

M114.6.p: An oath is sworn by touching a sacred thread.

M115.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone IV Nos. 6, 8, V No. 4.
M115.p: An oath is binding only if it is made in a specific formula; otherwise it is worthless.

M115.1.p: An oath is made three times over, making it especially binding.

M115.1.1.p: A threefold oath is so powerful that it dries up a stream, splits a rock in two, and makes a tree wither.

M116.p: An oath is taken on the hand of a saint.

M116.0.1.p: An oath is taken on the hand of a king.

M116.1.p: A person swears an oath on the staff (bachall) of a saint, which is held as a sacred object for binding promises.

M116.2.p: A person swears an oath on a saint's bell, using the bell as a sacred object to bind the promise.

M117.p: A person vows to do something, with the promise binding unless a catastrophe or world-ending disaster happens.

M118.p: A person swears an oath while holding or touching a skull.

M119.p: A general heading for vows and oaths that do not fit the more specific categories listed in the index.

M119.1.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Greek: Argonautica III 689, Odyssey V 185.
M119.1.p: A person swears by natural elements such as the sun, moon, stars, or wind.

M119.1.1.p: A person swears an oath by the River Styx, the river of the underworld in Greek myth.

M119.2.p: A person swears an oath by the gods of their clan or family group.

M119.3.r: Icelandic: Cleasby and Vigfússon Icel.— Eng. Dict. (1874) 853 s.v. “heitstrenging”; Lagerholm 18, *Boberg.
M119.3.p: Warriors or men make vows at the Yule festival, following an old Norse custom.

M119.4.p: A person makes a vow by placing a foot on a particular post in the hall.

M119.5.p: A person swears an oath while touching or resting a hand on a stone.

M119.6.p: A person swears an oath by a group of seven things that they serve.

M119.7.p: A person swears an oath by placing a hand on their genitals.

M119.8.p: A person swears an oath by the life of another person.

M119.8.1.p: A person swears an oath by the lives of their father and mother.

M119.8.2.p: A person swears an oath by the life of their father.

M120.p: A general heading for vows that concern how a person looks, such as hair, shaving, or clothing.

M121.r: *BP II 431ff.; A. Bugge “Harald Haarfagres løfte” Edda VII 166; Helm Altgermanische Religionsgeschichte I 301; Eitrem Opferritus und Voropfer (Skrifter Vidensk. Selsk. i Oslo No. 1, 1914) 400; Frazer Golden Bough III 194; Kruyt Het Animisme 33; FFC LXXXIII xxiv. — Irish: O’Suilleabhain 24, 45, Beal XXI 307, 316; Icelandic: *Boberg; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 308 No. 39; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 53 No. 400B*; Greek: Roscher Lexikon s.v. “Achilleus”; Jewish: *Neuman.
M121.p: A person vows not to shave or cut their hair until a set time has passed.

M122.p: A woman vows to keep her hair unbound until an enemy has been defeated.

M125.p: A person vows not to change their clothes until a set time has passed.

M126.p: A character swears not to wash their face or body until a set time has passed or a condition is met.

M130.p: A general heading for vows about sexual matters, such as chastity, marriage, or jealousy.

M131.r: Penzer I 67; Wesselski Mönchslatein 142 No. 117; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Greek: *Grote I 162f.
M131.p: A character swears to remain sexually abstinent, living without sex.

M132.p: A character swears to remain a virgin and never have sexual relations.

M133.p: A man swears that he will love and marry only a woman who is a virgin.

M134.p: A prince swears he will marry no woman unless he can beat her every day.

M135.p: A character swears never to marry again after a spouse dies or leaves.

M136.r: Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 71 (to Gonzenbach No. 32); *Roberts 137.
M136.p: A character swears not to marry until a pair of iron shoes wears out.

M137.r: Wells 64 (The Avowynge of King Arthur, etc.); Irish myth: *Cross.
M137.p: A husband swears he will never be jealous of his wife.

M137.1.p: A wife makes it a condition that her husband must be free from jealousy.

M138.p: A character vows to marry whoever first performs a certain act.

M138.1.p: A father vows to marry his two daughters to the first two men he sees the next morning.

M141.p: A character swears never to fight or struggle against a woman.

M142.p: A character swears never to carry a woman.

M145.p: A character vows not to marry any man who cannot perform a particular feat.

M145.1.p: A woman vows not to wed any man who is afraid to saddle and mount a lion.

M146.p: A character vows to marry a specific woman.

M146.1.p: A man vows to marry the queen of the fairies and will neither eat nor drink within her kingdom until this is accomplished.

M146.2.p: A boy vows to marry only a girl born under the same circumstances as himself.

M146.3.p: A vow that children conceived by magical means will marry, or become friends with, a certain person.

M146.4.p: A brother and sister arrange that their as-yet-unborn children will marry each other.

M146.5.p: A person swears to marry only the daughter of a particular man, and binds themselves to that promise.

M146.7.p: An enemy chief swears to marry the princess of the city he is besieging.

M149.p: A general group of miscellaneous vows concerning sex and marriage that do not fit the more specific categories.

M149.1.p: Two lovers promise each other that they will marry no one but each other.

M149.2.p: A person vows to die rather than marry a suitor they do not want.

M149.3.p: A person vows to kill a rival who is more successful in winning a lover.

M149.4.p: A quarreling prince and princess vow that if they marry, he will abandon her on the wedding day, and she will make him eat plain boiled rice and thin broth for six months.

M149.5.p: A person swears to marry their daughters only into families where each daughter gets a bridegroom, so that no daughter is left without a husband.

M149.6.p: A person vows to get a stubborn girl only half-married, meaning she is wed in some incomplete or partial way.

M149.7.p: A person vows to marry their daughter only to the man who kills a snake near her house.

M150.p: A general group of other vows and oaths that do not concern marriage or sex.

M151.r: Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight § 5; Irish myth: *Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
M151.p: A person vows not to eat until they have heard of an adventure or quest they are seeking.

M151.1.p: A person vows not to eat until they have learned a secret.

M151.2.p: A person vows not to marry until a quest has been completed.

M151.2.1.p: A person vows not to reign and to starve to death unless they find the original of a picture, which is the person shown in it.

M151.3.p: A person vows not to take food or drink until they learn how their father died.

M151.4.p: A person vows not to take food or drink until an enemy has been killed.

M151.5.p: A person vows not to eat or sleep until a certain event has come about.

M151.5.1.p: A person vows not to eat, drink, or move from their position until a dead hermit comes in person to accept a necklace.

M151.6.p: A person vows not to eat or drink until they know whether the king is still alive.

M151.7.p: A heroine vows not to laugh until the hero destined for her arrives.

M151.8.p: A person vows not to eat until a lost son has been found.

M151.9.p: A person vows not to see friends until a quest has been completed.

M152.p: A man vows not to sleep with his wife until an enemy has been killed.

M152.1.p: A person vows not to kiss anyone until his father has been avenged.

M152.2.p: A person vows not to sit in his father's high seat until the father has been avenged.

M155.p: A person makes a vow to perform some feat of bravery or daring.

M155.1.r: Wells 64 (The Avowynge of King Arthur, etc.).
M155.1.p: A person vows to kill a wild boar alone at night.

M155.2.p: A person vows to find a sister who has vanished.

M155.3.p: A person vows never to run away from fire or a weapon.

M156.p: A person vows to keep watch all night at a frightening place.

M157.r: Wells 64 (The Avowynge of King Arthur, etc.).
M157.p: A person vows to ride through the forest all night and kill every person he meets.

M158.r: Wells 64 (The Avowynge of King Arthur); Icelandic: Boberg.
M158.p: A person vows never to refuse food to any man.

M161.p: A person vows never to flee even in fear of death.

M161.1.p: A person vows to attack and kill the enemy or die trying.

M161.2.p: A person vows to avenge a king, friends, or father, or die in the attempt.

M161.3.p: A person vows to live and die with his king.

M161.4.r: (Cf. M165.) Hdwb. d. Märchens II s.v. “Gnade ausbitten”; Icelandic: Ragnars saga Loðbr. 139-41, *Boberg.
M161.4.p: A person vows to die on a spear rather than accept mercy.

M161.5.p: A person vows to die rather than serve the enemy.

M161.6.p: A person vows to die in battle rather than in bed.

M162.p: A person makes a vow that he will never be killed by just one opponent, so he can only be defeated by several at once.

M163.p: A person vows never to launch a surprise attack at night.

M164.p: A bard (professional poet or minstrel) vows that no member of his profession will ever ask anything of any man.

M165.p: A person vows never to ask anyone for peace or for mercy.

M166.p: A general heading for other vows concerning fighting and combat.

M166.1.p: A person vows to strike only one blow in a fight, never to attack a fallen enemy, and never to take his enemy's weapons.

M166.2.p: A person vows that he would rather be cut to pieces than let himself be tied up or bound.

M166.3.p: A person vows to kill anyone who touches his beard.

M166.4.p: A person vows never to fight against his brother.

M166.5.p: A person swears not to fight against the relatives of the king.

M167.p: A person vows to serve only the most generous of all kings.

M168.p: A person released from captivity vows not to lay waste to the country or take revenge on those who freed him.

M168.1.p: A person released from captivity vows not to deceive the man who spared his life.

M171.p: A person vows never to accept as a companion anyone who does not know any sport or game.

M172.p: A general heading for vows never to touch a certain thing.

M172.1.p: A person vows never to touch money and to give whatever anyone begs from him.

M172.2.p: A person vows never to touch a certain tree; later he cannot cross a bridge made of its wood.

M175.r: *Types 360, 1697; BP II 561ff.; Wesselski Mönchslatein 37 No. 44; India: *Thompson-Balys.
M175.p: Men make an agreement that each may say only a single phrase, and in keeping it they unwittingly confess to a crime.

M177.p: A person vows to change his religion.

M177.1.p: A person vows to become a Christian.

M177.1.1.p: A king vows to convert to Christianity if he wins a battle.

M177.1.2.p: A man vows not to be baptized until he has fought in seven battles for Jesus.

M177.2.p: A prince vows to serve the goddess Kali for the rest of his life.

M182.p: A person vows never to enter any house other than their own.

M183.p: A general heading for vows made to a god or in religious devotion.

M183.1.p: A person vows to build a shrine or temple.

M183.2.p: A person vows to bathe in the Ganges river, a sacred act of devotion.

M183.3.p: A knight vows not to return to the Round Table until he has found the Holy Grail.

M183.4.p: A condemned person vows to become a monk if he escapes execution.

M184.p: A ruler vows that if the queen gives birth to another girl, she and the child will both be killed.

M184.1.p: A chief vows that no daughter born to his wife will be allowed to live until she bears a son.

M185.p: A person vows to obey the laws.

M186.p: A person vows never to cross a boundary line into another's property.

M187.p: A person swears to accept whatever outcome a lottery or lot drawing produces.

M188.p: A person swears not to reveal what they have seen.

M192.p: A person vows to kill every king they meet, unless they are busy marrying a lady at that moment.

M193.p: A person vows to destroy a kingdom through severe self-denial and penance.

M200.p: A general heading for bargains and promises made between parties.

M201.p: A general heading for the making of bargains and promises.

M201.0.1.p: A holy man strikes a bargain with God.

M201.0.1.1.p: A covenant, or formal binding agreement, is made between Israel and God, with the bargain struck through a holy man.

M201.0.2.p: A formal covenant, or binding agreement, is made between a heathen (non-believer) and the Israelites.

M201.1.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 272ff., 1026; *Wilken Verspreide Geschriften I 539ff.; *W. Robertson Smith Religion of the Semites@3 270ff.; *Penzer I 98 n.; *Fb “skrive”; “blod” IV 47b; ** H. C. Turmbull The Blood Covenant (London, 1887).—Breton: Sébillot Incidents s.v. “sang”, “pacte”; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
M201.1.p: A binding agreement is sealed with blood, so the contract is written or signed in blood.

M201.1.1.p: The parties to a bargain mix their blood together to seal it.

M201.1.2.r: (Theophilus.) (Cf. M211.) Type 756B; *Andrejev FFC LXIX 64; Scala Celi 9a, 135b Nos 58, 749; Wünsche Teufel 55f.; England, U.S.: Baughman; Irish: Beal XXI 310 —312, O’Suilleabhain 33f.; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Argentina: Jijena Sanchez 80.
M201.1.2.p: A person signs a pact with the devil using their own blood.

M201.2.r: Hdwb. d. Abergl. II 272ff.; U.S.: Baughman; Africa (Fang): Nassau 242 No. 9.
M201.2.p: A covenant is confirmed by the parties eating a meal together.

M201.3.p: All parties spit into a vessel to seal a bargain.

M201.4.p: A covenant between saints is confirmed by cutting off their thumbs.

M201.5.p: A covenant or agreement is confirmed by a marriage.

M201.6.p: A covenant or agreement is confirmed by handing over hostages as security.

M202.p: A bargain or promise is carried out and kept as agreed.

M202.0.1.r: English romance: Malory VIII 30; Irish myth: *Cross.
M202.0.1.p: A bargain or promise must be fulfilled no matter what danger or cost it involves.

M202.1.p: A promise is to be fulfilled only when a pair of iron shoes wears out, meaning the promise will be kept after a very long time.

M202.2.p: A man keeps his word to return to his enemy if his mission to his own people fails.

M203.r: Basil Pentamerone I No. 5; Irish myth: *Cross; Missouri French: Carrière; Spanish Exempla: Keller; India: Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 560.
M203.p: A king's promise cannot be taken back or changed once made.

M203.1.p: A king punishes one of his own men who robs a person to whom the king has given safe conduct (a guarantee of safe passage).

M203.2.p: A king kills himself in order to carry out his own promise.

M203.3.p: A king sells himself and his family into slavery in order to keep a promise.

M204.p: A person who has been promised a boon or reward delays asking for it.

M204.1.r: English romance: Malory VIII 15; India: Thompson-Balys.
M204.1.p: Granted any wish, the recipient waits for a lucky or auspicious moment before announcing what he wants.

M205.p: A person fails to keep a bargain or promise they made.

M205.0.1.p: A promise is technically kept while its real purpose is betrayed, so the promiser escapes blame by a literal reading.

M205.1.p: An animal punishes a person who has broken a promise made to it.

M205.1.1.p: A turtle carries a man across water, then upsets him in revenge because he broke a promise made to it.

M205.1.1.1.r: Tahiti: Beckwith Myth 252; Tuamotu: Stimson MS (T-G. 3/600).
M205.1.1.1.p: A fish or whale carries a man over water, then shakes him off after the man strikes it on the head with a coconut.

M205.1.2.p: A cat that witnessed a man's betrothal later punishes him for breaking it by killing the son he had with another woman.

M205.2.p: A curse is laid on a person as the penalty for breaking a promise.

M205.3.p: A man who breaks an oath made to a woman is held to be unfit to rule as a rightful king.

M205.4.p: A king breaks his promise to look after a man's family, and is caught trying to steal the man's money.

M206.p: A promise made only as a polite formality, not seriously, does not bind the one who made it.

M206.1.p: A host, having praised a wine, promises to send his guest a cask of it, but later refuses, saying the promise was only a polite compliment.

M207.p: Bargains involving grants of land, where a ruler or owner gives land in exchange for something.

M208.p: A price is put on a person's head, offering a reward for capturing or killing them.

M210.r: Types 310, 313A, 316, 360, 400, 425C, 441, 500, 502, 706, 710, 756B, 810—812, 1170—1199; BP II 164, 329f., 427, 561ff., III 12, *Andrejev FFC LXIX 222ff.; *Fb “djævel” IV 99a, “blod” IV 47b.—England, U.S.: Baughman; Missouri French: Carrière; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; West Indies: Flowers 562.
M210.p: A person makes a bargain with the devil, trading something for the devil's help or favor.

M211.r: (Faust, Theophilus.) Types 330, 360, 361, 756B, 810, 812, 1170-1199; *BP II 164, 427, 561ff., III 12; *Andrejev FFC LXIX 46, 50, 223, 227 n.; Lidzbarski Am Urds-Brunnen IV 59 n. 1; Scala Celi 9a, 112a, 135b Nos. 58, 625, 749; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 667; *Fb “sjæl” III 215a; Faligan RTP V 1; Alphabet Nos. 50, 467; *Ludorff Anglia VII 60ff.; *Loomis White Magic 112f.; *K. Bittner Die Faustsage im russischen Schrifttum (Reichenberg. i. B. [Prager Deutsche Studien No. 37], 1925); *Krappe Bulletin Hispanique XXXIX 34.—Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3400, Legends No. 757; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 49, 67 Nos. 330, 510, Espinosa Jr. Nos. 70-74, 83f.; Italian Novella: Rotunda; Argentina: Jijena Sanchez 74; N. A. Indian (Wampanoag): Knight JAFL XXXVIII 134, (Salinan): Mason U Cal X 196.
M211.p: A man sells his soul to the devil in exchange for something.

M211.1.p: A man jokingly offers to sell his soul, not meaning it, but a devil in disguise takes him up on the offer and buys it.

M211.1.1.p: A man goes to a well at midnight on Old Christmas to see water turn into wine, and the devil seizes or injures him at the moment it happens.

M211.2.p: A man sells his soul to the devil in return for the devil building him a house, barn, or similar structure.

M211.3.p: A man leaves his soul to the devil in his will.

M211.4.p: Jews must repay the devil's help by yearly giving him a tribute of people.

M211.5.p: A man signs over his soul to the devil in exchange for something, with the exact wording of the contract being the point. The devil's terms and formula for the bargain are what matter here.

M211.6.p: A man trades his soul to the devil for a trip home in a boat that sails through the sky.

M211.7.p: A man sells his soul to the devil to gain magical power that lets him escape from anyone trying to catch him.

M211.8.p: A man sells his soul to the devil on condition that the devil performs one particular task for him.

M211.9.p: A person gives his soul to the devil in return for having wishes granted.

M212.p: The devil agrees to help a man commit robberies.

M212.1.r: They are his own weapons. Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 86.
M212.1.p: The devil, acting as a robber's helper, refuses to allow women's ornaments to be stolen.

M212.2.r: The man is hanged. *Krappe Archivum Romanicum VII 470ff.; *Wesselski Märchen 244 No. 54; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
M212.2.p: The devil, standing by the robber at the gallows, disowns the bargain he made with him. In the note, a ring the devil brings as a bribe turns into a rope, so the judge cannot find a rope and nearly frees the thief, believing a miracle has happened.

M213.p: The devil takes the place of a day laborer at mowing. He mows with a magic sickle, and the cruel overseer who tries to keep pace with him dies from exhaustion.

M214.p: The devil helps a gambler in exchange for the gambler performing one task for him each year.

M215.r: *Type 1186; **Taylor PMLA XXXVI 35ff., also in Bryan and Dempster Sources and Analogues of Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales 26974; *Herbert III 592; *Fb “ridefoged” III 53b; *Pauli (ed. Bolte) Nos. 81, 807; *Robinson Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer (Cambridge, Mass., 1933) 809 (Friar’s Tale).
M215.p: A judge is carried off by the devil because the devil takes only what is offered with the whole heart, and he hears the judge cursed for fraud with such sincerity that he takes him.

M216.p: The devil makes a bargain to help a man become a priest, on condition that the priest never later drives out devils from people.

M216.1.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3266, Legends Nos. 400ff.
M216.1.p: The devil helps a man study for the priesthood, but the man must promise his soul to the devil. Once he becomes a great priest, he finds a way to save himself.

M216.2.r: Is beaten. Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3269, Legends Nos. 413f.
M216.2.p: The devil makes a herdsman's son a priest in return for a whistle. After quarreling with the devil, who asks him to repair the whistle during Mass, the priest forgets everything he learned and cannot hold Mass.

M217.r: *Loomis White Magic 113; Alphabet No. 64; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 66 No. 508A*, Keller; Italian Novella: *Rotunda. Cf. Cosquin Études 545ff. (sale of self to magician).
M217.p: The devil makes a bargain to help a man win a woman.

M217.1.p: A servant makes a pact with the devil, denying Christ, to win a nobleman's daughter for himself.

M218.r: Dh I 140; Alphabet Nos. 64, 467; Irish: Beal XXI 311, O’Suilleabhain 33.
M218.p: A contract made with the devil is destroyed, so its terms no longer bind.

M218.1.p: Pacts with the devil, sealed in blood, are made ineffective by a saint.

M219.p: Other devil contract motifs that do not fit the more specific headings in this group.

M219.1.p: A bargain is made with the devil to obtain an heir, that is, a child.

M219.2.p: The devil comes to collect a man who has made a contract with him, taking him away at the agreed time.

M219.2.1.p: During a violent storm the devil appears and carries off the soul of a man bound to him by contract.

M219.2.2.p: The devil skins the dead body of a person who had made a contract with him.

M219.2.3.p: A man bound to the devil answers a summons by voice, saying the hour has come but he himself has not, so the devil cannot take him yet.

M219.2.4.p: The devil carries away a priest who loved hunting.

M219.2.5.p: The devil removes the body of his disciple from its coffin.

M219.2.6.p: The devil places the body of a man who had converted to him onto a sea monster, which carries it away.

M219.3.p: Familiar spirits guard and protect people who have made a pact with the devil.

M219.4.p: A familiar spirit devours anyone who fails to keep their pact with the devil.

M220.p: A general heading for other kinds of bargains and agreements, apart from those with the devil.

M221.r: **Kittredge Gawain and the Green Knight; Irish myth: *Cross.
M221.p: A bargain in which one party lets the other cut off his head, on the promise that the other will later let his own head be cut off in return.

M221.1.p: A hag offers to race men on the condition that whoever finishes last will be beheaded, and a marvelous runner defeats and beheads her.

M222.p: A man agrees to judge a quarrel between two animals in return for a promise that they will not eat him.

M223.r: English romance: Malory X 22; Irish myth: *Cross.
M223.p: Someone promises to grant a wish before hearing what it is, and is then bound to keep the promise.

M223.1.p: A person who never refuses any request, so anyone can ask anything of them.

M225.r: *Type 613; *BP II 468ff.; **Christiansen FFC XXIV 46, 54; *Fb “øje” III 1166b; Missouri French: Carrière; India: Thompson-Balys.
M225.p: A starving man agrees to have his eyes taken out in exchange for food.

M225.1.p: A rider trades away his horse, his clothes, and parts of his own body in exchange for food.

M226.p: A hero receives a magic shirt from a girl in return for agreeing to stay in Ireland for three years, and in return he claims her as his wife.

M231.p: A traveler gets free lodging at an inn in exchange for telling the innkeeper a good story.

M232.p: A prince agrees to forfeit his life if he fails to learn a secret, in exchange for the chance to learn it.

M233.p: Three deformed witches are invited to a wedding in return for helping someone. The bargain is that they receive the invitation in exchange for their aid.

M234.p: A person's life is spared on condition that they serve the one who spared them for the rest of their life.

M234.1.p: A life is spared in exchange for a gift of poetic mead, a sacred intoxicating drink.

M234.2.r: Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 83 f. (Thor and Loki).
M234.2.p: A person's life is spared because they bring a feared enemy to the spot without carrying a weapon.

M234.3.p: A life is bought back with gold, so the person is allowed to live in exchange for payment.

M234.4.p: A life is bought by promising to pay compensation and to heal the enemy who was harmed.

M235.p: A woman agrees to ride naked through the streets as the price of freeing the citizens from something.

M236.p: Peace is obtained for a husband through a bargain, so that he is spared harm.

M237.p: A bargain is struck so that one party can avoid public shame or loss of honor.

M237.1.p: Opponents agree not to fight, and so neither side is defeated.

M241.p: Two partners make a bargain to divide everything they win between them equally.

M241.1.r: *Type 505—508; *BP III 490; Köhler-Bolte I 11, 444; *Liljeblad Tobiasgeschichte; English: Wells 160 (Sir Amadace); India: Thompson-Balys.
M241.1.p: Under the agreement to divide winnings, one partner demands half of the bride as his share. When the hero shows he is willing to keep the bargain, his helper gives in.

M241.2.r: *Type 1364; Wesselski Märchen 187 No. 2; English: Wells 55 (Sir Gawayne and the Green Knight).
M241.2.p: After agreeing to divide all winnings, one man receives favors such as gifts and kisses from the other man's wife, and he faithfully carries them back to her husband.

M242.p: Mortals make bargains and promises with supernatural beings.

M242.1.p: A mortal raises a fairy child to prevent the child's destruction of the crops.

M242.2.p: A hungry god agrees with an untouchable man that he will eat food only if it is given by the man's own hands.

M242.3.p: An ogre is released in return for giving up his magic girdle.

M244.p: People make bargains and promises with animals.

M244.1.p: A bargain is made with the king of the mice.

M244.2.p: A captured bird promises to bring fifteen other birds in return for its freedom.

M246.p: Two parties swear a pact of friendship, binding themselves to one another in a lasting alliance.

M246.1.p: Two animals make a pact of friendship and agree to stand by each other.

M246.1.1.p: An elephant and a jackal swear friendship with each other.

M246.1.2.p: A louse and a crow swear friendship with each other.

M246.2.p: Two families agree that whatever the poverty of one family's son, the other family's daughter will still accept him as her husband.

M246.3.p: Two friends make a pact to help each other find wives, so that each secures a bride for the other.

M250.p: Promises that are made in connection with a person's death, such as vows about what will happen after it.

M251.p: A promise made by a dying man is carried out faithfully by the one who gave his word.

M252.r: (Or two friends agree that the first to die shall bring news.) *Type 470; Swiss: Jegerlehner Oberwallis 305 No. 6, 323 Nos. 112, 113, 329 Nos. 31, 33; Irish: Beal XXI 331f., O’Suilleabhain 99—102, *Cross; Jewish: bin Gorion Born Judas VI 123, 311.
M252.p: A dying man promises to send word back from the other world, and tries to bring news of what lies beyond death.

M253.r: *Type 470; Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 561; **MacKay The Double Invitation; Jewish Neuman.
M253.p: Two friends remain bound together even in death, so that the one who is still alive follows the other into the land of the dead to keep the pledge.

M254.p: A man promises to be buried together with his wife if she dies before him.

M255.r: *Type 510B; *Cox 53—79 passim; De Vries Studien over Færösche Balladen 133; Icelandic: Boberg; Danish: Grundtvig No. 135.
M255.p: A dying wife makes her husband promise not to remarry unless his new bride meets conditions she sets out, and he agrees.

M256.p: Someone breaks a promise made to a dying man.

M256.1.r: “If he is in Hell it will do him no good; if he is in Heaven he won’t need it; and if he is in Purgatory he can purge himself.” Italian Novella: Rotunda.
M256.1.p: Sons fail to keep their promise to pay for masses for their dead father's soul.

M257.r: Köhler-Bolte I 117; Gascon: Bladé I 3, 181; India: Thompson-Balys.
M257.p: A dying monster asks for something to be done after its death, and promises good results in return: the hero must eat parts of its body, which will give him great strength and bring his wife children with great powers.

M257.1.p: A dying hero makes a request of his disciples, and promises them something in return for carrying it out.

M257.2.p: A murdered person makes a request of the one who killed him and promises something in return for granting it.

M258.p: A promise made to a dying man must be kept, and keeping it is seen as sacred.

M258.1.p: A promise made to a dying father sends the one who made it on a series of adventures.

M258.2.p: A dying father makes his son promise never to marry a woman from a certain tribe.

M258.3.p: A dying father makes his child promise to bury him back in his homeland, and the promise to a dying man is treated as binding.

M260.p: A general category of promises or pledges that do not fit the more specific promise motifs listed under this heading.

M261.r: Robinson Complete Works of Geoffrey Chaucer (Cambridge, Mass., 1933) 826 (Franklin’s Tale); **Dempster and Tatlock in Bryan and Dempster Sources and Analogues of Chaucer’s Canterbury Tales 333—56; Irish myth: Cross; cf. Type 976.
M261.p: A chaste woman vows to marry her lover once the rocks leave the coast, a promise that can only be kept if magic moves the rocks.

M261.1.p: A chaste woman promises to marry her lover if he can make a garden bloom in winter.

M261.1.1.p: A raja promises to marry a girl when a cut mango branch blooms.

M261.2.p: A princess promises to embrace her teacher on her wedding day, but the teacher has only been testing her promise.

M262.p: A man promises to have only one wife if he is cured of an illness.

M263.p: A host agrees to march his army back a day's journey if a warrior stops his attacks until a certain future battle.

M266.r: Danish: Kristensen Danske Sagn III (1895) 145ff., (1931) 107ff.; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 134 No. 85; Italian Novella: Rotunda; West Indies: Flowers 562.
M266.p: A man promises to build a church if he is saved from drowning or danger at sea.

M267.p: A man promises to give another man's wife to someone for a day.

M268.p: A marriage is promised in return for saving someone's life.

M271.p: Sons agree to meet at their father's grave after a year away in the world learning a trade.

M272.p: A supernatural woman promises to return to her human husband if she gives birth to a boy.

M290.p: A general category of bargains and promises that do not fit the more specific motifs listed under this heading.

M291.p: A trickster makes impossible bargains and still collects his payment, trusting that within the agreed year one of the parties will die.

M292.p: A wife takes on her husband's penances, even going to heaven in his place, until he dreams of her reward and rejects the bargain.

M293.p: A covenant under which one nation agrees not to take a city from its people without their consent.

M294.p: God promises not to destroy a sinful city if righteous people live there.

M295.p: A bargain in which one party agrees to keep a secret.

M295.1.p: A tiger lets a man go on condition that he does not tell anyone what he has overheard.

M296.p: Two men who are both in love with the same girl promise each other not to deal with her unless the other agrees.

M300.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics s.v. “Divination”; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 326, 334f.; Schott Weissagen und Erfüllung im deutschen Volksmärchen (München, 1936).
M300.p: Stories in which someone foretells what will happen in the future.

M300.1.r: So it was. Irish myth: Cross.
M300.1.p: Jesus prophesies that certain people will stay alive until Saint Patrick comes.

M300.2.p: Someone makes a prophecy without knowing or meaning to.

M300.3.p: A person gains the gift of prophecy from another prophet.

M300.4.p: A prophecy is prevented from being spoken or made known.

M301.r: **E. Bass Die merkmale der israelitischen Prophetie nach der traditionellen Auffassung des Talmud (Berlin, 1917); *Hdwb. d. Abergl. IX Nachträge 66—100; Icelandic: *Boberg; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
M301.p: Stories about prophets, people who foretell the future, of many kinds.

M301.0.1.p: A prophet is fated never to be believed, even when speaking the truth.

M301.0.2.p: A prophet speaks prophecies on six nights of each year.

M301.1.p: A wild man, a savage or forest dweller, serves as a prophet.

M301.2.p: An old woman serves as a prophet.

M301.2.1.r: Type 516; *Cosquin Études 555; *Köhler in Gonzenbach I 209ff.; *BP IV 189; *Penzer Pentamerone of Basile (London, 1932) I 11; Penzer Ocean V 171; Rösch FFC LXXVII 100; Icelandic: *Boberg.
M301.2.1.p: An old woman, enraged after a young man has accidentally knocked her over, curses him with a prophecy about his future.

M301.2.2.p: A völva, a seeress, prophesies the child's future at its birth.

M301.3.p: Druids serve as prophets who foretell the future.

M301.4.p: An old man who writes in a book makes prophecies.

M301.5.p: Saints, or holy men, serve as prophets who foretell the future.

M301.5.1.p: An anchorite, a hermit living in seclusion, prophesies at a childbirth.

M301.5.2.p: Cuchulinn prophesies that fifty women will give birth to children who will be loyal to God.

M301.6.p: Fairies serve as prophets who foretell the future.

M301.6.1.p: Banshees, female fairies of Irish folklore, appear as signs that misfortune or death is coming.

M301.7.p: A biblical figure who is counted as a prophet, someone who foretells the future or speaks for God.

M301.7.1.p: Moses is recognized as a prophet who foretells events or speaks God's word.

M301.7.2.p: King David is recognized as a prophet who foretells events.

M301.7.3.p: Abraham is recognized as a prophet. In a Jewish tradition the note identifies this with a particular source, the Neuman reference.

M301.8.p: A prophecy is given by a personified abstraction, such as Death, Fortune, or a similar figure speaking as a person.

M301.9.p: A half-wit or simpleton is regarded as a prophet, so that his foolish words turn out to foretell the future.

M301.9.1.p: A fool or jester, a paid entertainer, is regarded as a prophet whose jokes or foolish speech foretell events.

M301.10.r: (Cf. V230.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Boberg; Jewish: Neuman.
M301.10.p: Angels act as prophets, delivering predictions of what will happen.

M301.11.p: A spirit acts as a prophet, foretelling what will happen.

M301.12.r: Icelandic: Corpus Poeticum Boreale I 131, FFC LXXIII xxxvii, *Boberg.
M301.12.p: Three fates, called norns, foretell the destiny of a child when it is born.

M301.13.p: Icelandic guardian spirits, called spádísir, foretell that victory will come to someone.

M301.14.p: A dead person is summoned and then gives a prophecy about the future.

M301.15.p: A mountain takes human form and prophesies the death of a whole family.

M301.16.p: Gods foretell both good and bad things about a hero's fate.

M301.17.p: A king is regarded as a prophet who foretells events.

M301.17.1.p: In his will, a king foretells that the daughters of his son will be fruitful and have many children.

M301.18.p: A poet is regarded as a prophet who foretells the future.

M301.19.p: A smith, or metalworker, is regarded as a prophet who foretells the future.

M301.20.p: A child is regarded as a prophet who foretells what will happen.

M301.21.p: A sibyl, a female prophet, writes her prophecies on leaves, which the winds blow about and scatter.

M302.p: A general category of ways a person can foretell the future, such as reading signs, stars, dreams or the body.

M302.1.r: Type 516; Rösch FFC LXXVII 116; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 87 n. 3.
M302.1.p: A person learns what will happen by understanding the speech of animals and hearing what they say.

M302.2.p: A person's destiny is believed to be written on the skull, so that reading the bones reveals what will happen to him.

M302.2.1.p: A person's fate is written on the top of the head, and anyone who can read it can foretell his life.

M302.2.2.p: A person's destiny can be read from the features of his face.

M302.3.r: Vergil Aeneid Book 6; Icelandic: MacCulloch Eddic 127.
M302.3.p: A person goes down into hell to find out what the future holds.

M302.4.r: *Prato RTP IV 178; *Wesselofsky Romania VI (1877) 161ff.; *Patch Fortuna 76—78 and notes; Dickson 33 n. 15; Fb “lykkestjærne” II 477, “stjærne” III 577b; *Hdwb. d. Abergl. VIII 461ff., IX N. 596—762; *Loomis White Magic 52. — Irish: Cross, Beal XXI 313; Icelandic: *Boberg; Italian Novella: *Rotunda; Jewish: *Neuman; Chinese: Graham.
M302.4.p: A person's future is predicted by casting a horoscope based on the positions of the stars.

M302.4.1.p: A ruler or authority forbids the practice of astrology, so that people may not read the stars to foretell the future.

M302.5.p: A person is given difficult tasks in order to learn from how they turn out what the future holds.

M302.6.p: A prophecy is written on a well, where it can be read to learn what will happen.

M302.7.p: A person learns what will happen in the future through a dream.

M302.8.p: A person learns the future by reading a prophecy in a book.

M303.p: A person's future is foretold by reading the lines of the palm of the hand.

M304.p: A prediction is made from someone's mysterious or cryptic laugh, which is taken as a sign of what will happen.

M305.r: Dickson 132 n. 108; Frazer Apollodorus I 285 n. 4; Gaster Oldest Stories 205; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman.
M305.p: An oracle gives a prophecy that can be understood in more than one way, so that its true meaning becomes clear only later.

M306.p: A prophecy is given in riddling or puzzling words whose meaning is hard to grasp until events make it clear.

M306.1.r: (Thou shalt have children and they shall not die, etc.) Jewish: Neuman, Gaster Exempla 217 No. 144, Gaster Oldest Stories 205.
M306.1.p: A riddling prophecy says that what one sows one shall not reap, and similar cryptic sayings, whose meaning is unclear at first.

M306.2.p: A couple is told by a prophecy that one son will become a purse cutter (a thief) and the other a killer, and the wife says they will make one a purse designer and the other a butcher.

M306.3.p: A prophecy says a princess will marry a man who is a physician, a fisherman and a prince all in one, and a man fulfills this by putting on the guise of all three, one on top of another.

M306.4.p: A riddling prophecy warns that the one who will kill you will grow up in a certain place named Braja.

M306.5.p: An ambiguous prophecy, worded so that its meaning is hidden or puzzling, that a person will kill a child who is not present but is somewhere in the village. The riddling wording is the point, and the prophecy often sets up a later twist.

M310.p: A general heading for prophecies that foretell good fortune or a bright future for someone.

M310.1.p: A prophecy that a person will become great and famous in the future.

M310.1.1.p: A prophecy that a person's descendants will rise to preeminence, being greater or more honored than others.

M310.1.1.1.p: A prophecy that a man's descendants will be preeminent, but only if they do the will of a saint who is yet to be born.

M311.r: (Cf. M301.2.2, M301.5.1, M301.12, M359.3, M371.1.) Gaster Exempla 229 No. 242 (Moses); Wells 103 (Alliterative Alexander Fragment); Loomis White Magic 16f.; Irish myth: *Cross; Danish: Grundtvig No. 42; Icelandic: Boberg; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Greek: Frazer Apollodorus I 24 n. 1 (Zeus and Mitis), Roscher Lexikon s.v. “Achilleus”; India: *Thompson-Balys.
M311.p: A general heading for prophecies that a child not yet born will achieve greatness.

M311.0.1.p: A prophecy that a newborn child will lead a heroic life.

M311.0.2.p: A prophecy that a hero will be born at a certain time or in a certain place.

M311.0.2.1.p: A prophecy that a hero will be conceived at a certain time.

M311.0.3.p: A prophecy that a child will be born.

M311.0.3.1.p: A prophecy that a childless couple will have a child.

M311.0.3.2.p: A prophecy that a raja who takes one more wife will have a son.

M311.0.4.p: Heavenly voices announce that a future child who will be a hero is being born.

M311.1.p: A prophecy that a king's grandson will overthrow him and take his throne.

M311.2.p: A prophecy that a child born at a certain time will build a church or other religious building.

M311.3.r: Loomis White Magic 17f.; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 327, O’Suilleabhain 74.
M311.3.p: A prophecy that an unborn child will become a saint.

M311.4.p: A prophecy that an unborn child will become king.

M311.5.p: A prophecy that an unborn child will become the deliverer of his nation.

M311.6.p: A prophecy that an unborn child will become a prophet.

M312.r: *Types 461, 517, 725, 930; *BP I 322; English romance: Malory XI 4; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 531; Korean: Zong in-Sob 72 No. 39, 209 No. 98.
M312.p: A prophecy that a young person will achieve future greatness.

M312.0.1.r: *Type 725; *BP I 324; Cox 500; MacCulloch Childhood 354; Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
M312.0.1.p: A dream foretells that the dreamer, or a child, will grow up to achieve great things.

M312.0.2.p: Animals foretell that a child will grow up to be great.

M312.0.3.p: A prophecy promises great future success to a boy, but only if he survives to age eighteen.

M312.0.4.p: The mother has a symbolic dream or vision showing that her unborn child will be great.

M312.0.4.1.p: The mother dreams of a tree that grows enormously, signalling that her child will be a hero or saint.

M312.0.5.p: A prophecy says the son will one day tie his father to a horse's leg and beat him fifty times.

M312.1.r: *Types 461, 930; **Aarne FFC XXIII; **Tille Zs. f. Vksk. XXVIII 22a; India: Thompson-Balys.
M312.1.p: A prophecy says a poor boy will marry into wealth.

M312.1.1.p: A prophecy says a poor girl will marry into wealth.

M312.2.r: (Vaticinium.) *Type 517; *BP I 324; Köhler-Bolte I 145, 430; *Wesselski Märchen 221 No. 35; Campbell Sages cxii; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
M312.2.p: A prophecy says the child's parents will one day bow down or submit to their son.

M312.2.1.p: A prophecy says the son will become more powerful than his father.

M312.2.2.p: A prophecy says the youngest brother will one day rule over his older brothers.

M312.3.r: *Type 567; *BP III 3; **Aarne MSFO XXV 176; Chauvin VI 170; India: *Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1138; Indonesia: De Vries’s list No. 190.
M312.3.p: Whoever eats the heart of a magic bird will become rich, or become a king.

M312.3.1.p: Whoever eats a magic fish will be able to spit out treasure.

M312.3.2.p: Whoever eats the outside of a certain fruit will become king, and whoever eats its seed will drop gems from his mouth whenever he laughs.

M312.4.p: A prophecy says a girl will grow up to be extraordinarily beautiful.

M312.5.p: A prophecy says the child will one day build a church or other religious building.

M312.6.p: A prophecy says the boys will become fathers of saints.

M312.7.p: A prophecy promises good luck to a child who has been cast out or rejected.

M312.8.p: A prophecy says a man will be able to make the sun and moon stand still.

M312.9.p: A prophecy says no people or king will be able to resist the hero.

M313.p: A man who has been turned into a pig becomes human again after he marries for the third time.

M314.p: A prophecy foretells that a man, while still a child, will grow up to become king.

M314.0.1.p: A prophecy foretells that a girl will become queen.

M314.1.p: A prophecy says that the son who catches a certain fawn will become king.

M314.2.p: A prophecy says a king will be succeeded by whichever son he sees first. The king sends for his elder son, who is delayed, so the younger son arrives first; the elder son is killed the next day and the younger son becomes king.

M314.3.p: A prophecy says that a younger son will succeed to the throne.

M314.4.p: A prophecy promises a fugitive hero that he will one day rule a great empire.

M315.p: A prophecy says that a man will eat a magic salmon and gain knowledge.

M316.p: A prophecy says that strength will be gained by drinking milk from the hero's skull.

M317.p: A prophecy says that the family or race will never lack an illustrious woman.

M318.p: A prophecy says that Ireland will have no snakes.

M318.1.p: A prophecy says that Israel will have no snakes.

M321.p: A prophecy promises a person a long life.

M321.1.p: A saint blesses a family so that the blessing passes down from generation to generation.

M322.p: A prophecy says that a person will take revenge for his own death after he is dead.

M323.r: Irish myth: Cross; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 183.
M323.p: A prophecy says that a person will win a victory despite overwhelming odds.

M324.p: A prophecy foretells a future Golden Age, a time of great happiness.

M325.p: A prophecy foretells that a people will enjoy glory and prosperity.

M326.r: Eskimo (West Hudson Bay): Boas BAM XV 343.
M326.p: A prophecy says that a person will become a successful hunter.

M331.p: A prophecy or foretelling says that a princess will marry a prince.

M340.p: A general category of prophecies that foretell bad outcomes for the person concerned.

M340.1.p: A prophecy of grief comes true when a relative or friend of the person dies.

M340.2.p: A prophecy that is forced out of someone, such as by compulsion, is unfavorable in its content.

M340.3.p: A prophecy at a child's birth says the newborn will suffer misfortune in general.

M340.4.p: A prophecy warns that a bridegroom will meet disaster if he rides a particular elephant that comes to meet him.

M340.5.p: Someone foretells that danger lies ahead.

M340.6.p: Someone foretells a great misfortune coming to the person.

M341.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die.

M341.0.1.p: A saint prophesies that a certain man will receive a warning before he dies.

M341.0.2.p: A prophecy says all forty of a man's sons will die at the same moment.

M341.0.3.p: A prophecy of death will not come true if the baby is married to a girl of twelve years.

M341.1.r: Irish: Beal XXI 313, O’Suilleabhain 37, *Cross; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
M341.1.p: A prophecy says a person will die at, before, or within a certain time.

M341.1.1.p: A prophecy says a person will die on the day of their wedding.

M341.1.1.1.p: A prophecy says a person will die within a year after marrying.

M341.1.1.2.p: A prophecy says a person will die on the seventh day of marriage.

M341.1.1.3.p: A prophecy says a father will die when his daughter marries.

M341.1.1.4.p: A prophecy says a person will die upon entering the marriage chamber.

M341.1.2.p: A prophecy says a person will die early.

M341.1.2.1.p: A prophecy says a king will die before the next morning.

M341.1.2.2.p: A prophecy says a person will die on the twelfth day after birth.

M341.1.2.3.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die within two months. The prophecy sets a short, fixed deadline on the person's life.

M341.1.2.4.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die three years and three months from now. The prophecy sets a specific short lifespan.

M341.1.2.5.p: A prophecy declares that a newborn baby will live only seven days. The child's life is foretold to be very brief.

M341.1.3.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die before reaching a certain age. The exact age is set by the particular tale.

M341.1.3.1.p: A prophecy foretells that a child will be hanged before turning fifteen. The child's death by hanging is fated before that age.

M341.1.3.2.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die before reaching eighteen years of age.

M341.1.4.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die at a certain specific age.

M341.1.4.1.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die at the age of sixteen.

M341.1.4.2.p: A prophecy warns that a newborn boy will be in danger in his eighteenth year. The threat is fixed to that age.

M341.1.4.3.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die when they are twenty-five years old.

M341.1.4.3.1.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die on their twenty-first birthday. This is a specific form of the twenty-five-year prophecy.

M341.1.4.4.p: A prophecy foretells that a man will hang himself when he is thirty years old.

M341.1.4.5.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die at the age of sixty.

M341.1.5.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die within a certain period of time. The period is set by the particular tale.

M341.1.5.1.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die in ten years.

M341.1.5.2.p: A prophecy declares that the hero will not live another eighteen years.

M341.1.6.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die only after a certain long time has passed.

M341.1.6.1.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die only after three life spans have passed.

M341.1.6.2.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die only after two life spans have passed.

M341.1.6.3.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die only after a three-year dominion, that is, a three-year rule.

M341.1.7.p: A prophecy foretells that a child will die at birth or very soon after. The prediction is made about the infant's death in the early stage of life.

M341.1.7.1.p: A prophecy says a person will die at the sight of his son before the son reaches twelve years old. The father's death is tied to seeing the boy at that age.

M341.2.r: *Basset 1001 Contes II 209; *Krappe Scandinavian Studies 16 (1942) 20—35; Irish myth: *Cross, India: Thompson-Balys; Japanese: Ikeda.
M341.2.p: A prophecy says a person will die by a particular instrument or means. The death happens exactly as foretold even though the person takes every precaution to avoid it.

M341.2.0.1.p: A prophecy says a person will be killed by a particular weapon. The foretold weapon is the means of death.

M341.2.1.r: *Frazer Golden Bough X—XI (Balder the Beautiful); Icelandic: *Boberg.
M341.2.1.p: A prophecy says a person will die from mistletoe. The plant is the foretold cause of death.

M341.2.2.p: A prophecy says a person will die in a storm. The storm is the foretold cause of death.

M341.2.3.p: A prophecy says a person will drown. Drowning is the foretold cause of death.

M341.2.3.1.r: Irish: Beal XXI 328, O’Suilleabhain 87; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 136 No. 95; India: Thompson-Balys.
M341.2.3.1.p: A prophecy of death by drowning is fulfilled when a man, while drinking water, chokes and strangles to death. The water he drinks is the instrument of his death.

M341.2.4.r: It so happens. *Jackson The Motive of the Threefold Death in the Story of Suibhne Geilt (Essays and Studies Presented to Eoin MacNeill 535—550); Irish myth: *Cross; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 136 No. 96; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
M341.2.4.p: A prophecy says a child will die three different ways: from hunger, from fire, and from water. The child's death is foretold as a combination of these three causes.

M341.2.5.r: **Taylor MPh XIX 93ff.; Krappe PSASS XVII (1942-43) 20ff.; Icelandic: Boberg.
M341.2.5.p: A prophecy says a man will be killed by a horse's head. The horse's head is the foretold instrument of his death.

M341.2.6.r: Type 333*; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 166*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV 136 No. 94.
M341.2.6.p: A prophecy says a person will be killed by a wolf. The death is by a wolf's claw, or by a cat that has been transformed into a wolf.

M341.2.7.p: A prophecy says a person will die by fire. Fire is the foretold cause of death.

M341.2.7.1.p: A prophecy says that sinners will be burned by fire on Doomsday, the day of judgment. The fire is the foretold punishment at the end of time.

M341.2.8.p: A prophecy says a person will die by poison. Poison is the foretold cause of death.

M341.2.9.r: Greek: *Frazer Apollodorus I 94 n. 1 (Jason); India: Thompson-Balys.
M341.2.9.p: A prophecy says a person will be killed by a man wearing only one sandal. The man with one sandal is the foretold killer.

M341.2.10.p: A prophecy says a person will die from the bite of a stone lion. In the tale, a scorpion hidden inside the statue kills the man.

M341.2.10.1.p: A prophecy of death by a stone lion is fulfilled by a tiger. A tiger-shaped cake becomes a real tiger and kills the man, despite all precautions.

M341.2.10.2.r: India: *Thompson-Balys; Korean: Zong in-Sob 51 No. 30, 58 No. 33.
M341.2.10.2.p: A prophecy of death is fulfilled when a tiger picture comes to life and kills the man.

M341.2.11.r: Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 932*; Estonian: Aarne FFC XXV No. 932*; Russian: Andrejev No. 932*; Spanish: Boggs FFC XC 62 No. 449*.
M341.2.11.p: A prophecy says a person will be killed by lightning. Lightning is the foretold cause of death.

M341.2.12.p: A prophecy says a woman will die through her future husband. The husband is the foretold cause of her death.

M341.2.13.p: A prophecy says a person will die because of a spindle wound, meaning they will be pricked or wounded by a spindle.

M341.2.14.r: Italian: Basile Pentamerone II No. 8, III No. 3, V No. 5.
M341.2.14.p: A prophecy says a person will die through a bone, such as being killed or harmed by a bone.

M341.2.15.r: Russian: Afanasief “Tale of Prince Arta” (Moscow, 1897) 149 (cited in von Sydow Fåvne 45).
M341.2.15.p: A prophecy says a person will be killed by a man who has a certain name, so the name itself marks the killer.

M341.2.16.p: A prophecy says a person will die from thorns found in their rice.

M341.2.17.p: A prophecy says a king will be slain by a certain spear, unless that spear is handed over whenever it is demanded.

M341.2.18.p: A prophecy says a person will die in battle.

M341.2.18.1.p: Because of a prophecy that he will be slain in battle, a hero is kept from going to war.

M341.2.19.p: A prophecy says a person will die at the hands of a certain other person.

M341.2.20.p: A prophecy says a huge wheel will roll over Europe and slaughter people on a massive scale.

M341.2.21.p: A prophecy says a person will die from a snakebite.

M341.2.21.1.p: A prophecy, revealed in a dream, says a person will die from a cobra's bite.

M341.2.22.p: A prophecy says a person will die by a calf.

M341.2.23.p: A prophecy says a person will die by hanging.

M341.2.24.p: A prophecy says a person will die by an alligator or crocodile.

M341.2.25.p: A prophecy says a man will be swallowed up by the earth at the foot of his stairs.

M341.2.26.p: A prophecy says a king's son will die for lack of water.

M341.3.p: A prophecy says a person will die in a particular place.

M341.3.1.p: A prophecy says a person will die in Jerusalem.

M341.3.2.p: A prophecy says a person will die between two hills called Erin and Alba, and the man dies between two hills so named.

M341.3.3.p: A prophecy says a person will drown in a particular stream.

M341.3.4.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will die on a seashore.

M341.4.p: A condemned criminal, on his way to execution, predicts that the judge or king who sentenced him will soon meet him in death.

M341.5.p: A prophecy says that either a young child or its mother will die.

M341.6.p: A person foretells the date or manner of his own death.

M343.p: A prophecy says a child will kill his father, and despite all efforts to prevent it, the child does so.

M343.0.2.p: A prophecy says that a mother will be killed by her own children.

M343.3.p: A prophecy says a man will be murdered by his nephew.

M343.4.p: A prophecy says that a wicked husband and wife will be killed by their own child.

M343.5.p: A prophecy says that a person will be killed by his parents.

M345.1.p: A prophecy says a girl will have a hundred lovers, will marry her servant, and will die from a spider bite.

M345.1.1.p: A prophecy says a woman will have many lovers.

M345.2.p: A prophecy warns that a man will deceive many women. It is a foretelling of a man's future treachery toward women.

M346.p: A prophecy says that a child will be kidnapped or carried off at a certain time. The child's fate is foretold as an abduction.

M348.p: A murderer is warned by a voice from God that the murder will be avenged. The warning tells him he will be punished for his crime.

M351.r: (Baarlam and Josaphat.) *Cosquin Études 27ff.; Ward II 111ff.; Spanish Exempla: Keller.
M351.p: A prophecy foretells that a young man will give up his religion and become a Christian.

M352.p: A prophecy warns a prince of particular dangers that will befall him during his journey to his wedding.

M353.r: (She disenchants him from magic sleep.) *Cosquin Contes indiens 108ff.; India: Thompson-Balys.
M353.p: A bird predicts that a girl will have a dead husband. The bird's words foretell her future widowhood.

M354.p: A prophecy says that a child will have an external soul, meaning that his life is bound up with an object or creature kept hidden outside his body.

M354.1.p: A prophecy foretells that the child will be reborn as a monkey after death.

M355.p: A prophecy says that an unborn child will be blind, deformed, sickly, or otherwise afflicted.

M356.p: Prophecies are made about the destiny of a country, foretelling bad fortune for the nation.

M356.1.p: Prophecies foretell how a war will turn out, usually for the worse.

M356.1.1.p: A prophecy foretells that a side will lose a battle or combat.

M356.1.2.p: Prophecies foretell what will happen to particular heroes in battle, such as whether they will die or survive.

M356.1.3.p: A prophecy says that whichever side first kills an enemy in battle will be defeated.

M356.1.4.p: A prophecy foretells that a fortress will be destroyed.

M356.2.p: A prophecy foretells a plague, described as a flame of fire, that will destroy three-fourths of the population of Ireland. The plague can be prevented by fasting and similar measures.

M356.3.p: A prophecy says that an unborn or newborn girl will bring evil upon the land.

M356.4.p: A prophecy foretells that evil will come to a country.

M356.5.p: A prophecy foretells the end of the Round Table fellowship of King Arthur's knights.

M357.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 501.
M357.p: A prophecy foretells a catastrophe that will destroy the world.

M357.1.p: A prophecy says a fiery bolt from a dragon will kill most of the world's people.

M358.p: A group of prophecies that foretell things about a person's journeys, and these are bad ones.

M358.1.p: Prophecies that predict evil or harm will come to someone who travels.

M358.1.1.p: A prophecy says that a person will die while on a journey.

M358.2.p: A prophecy foretells that someone will make a journey to the otherworld, the realm of the dead or of spirits.

M359.p: A group of miscellaneous bad prophecies that do not fit into the more specific categories.

M359.1.p: A prophecy says the weapons that will kill a man will later tell his son how he died.

M359.2.p: A prophecy says a prince will marry a commoner, a woman of humble birth.

M359.3.p: A prophecy says a child not yet born will grow up to kill an enemy as revenge.

M359.4.p: A prophecy says someone will be tortured in many different painful ways.

M359.5.p: A prophecy says a person will be poor from the moment of birth.

M359.6.p: A prophecy says all of a person's animals, such as flocks, will die and his family will die too.

M359.7.p: A prophecy says a rich man will have a son, but the son will marry a poor girl.

M359.8.p: A prophecy foretells a great flood that will cover the land.

M359.9.p: A prophecy foretells a famine, a time of extreme hunger and lack of food.

M359.10.p: A prophecy says that a person is destined from birth to become a thief.

M360.p: A general group of prophecies that do not fall under the other headings of prophecy.

M361.r: Dickson 132 n. 108; Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Sturlaugs saga Starfsama; India: Thompson-Balys.
M361.p: A hero is fated by prophecy, and only this one particular hero will be able to succeed in the exploit.

M361.1.p: A prophecy says that a certain hero will be the one to achieve the Holy Grail.

M362.r: Spanish Exempla: Keller; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
M362.p: A prophecy says a ruler must die for his side to win the victory.

M363.p: A prophecy that a future religious leader will come.

M363.1.p: A prophecy that Christ will come.

M363.1.1.p: A prophecy that the Antichrist, an enemy of Christ, will come.

M363.2.p: A prophecy that the Messiah will come.

M363.2.1.p: A prophecy that a certain woman will be the ancestress of King David and of the Messiah.

M364.p: A group of miscellaneous prophecies connected with saints or holy men.

M364.1.p: A prophecy that a saint's monastery will be persecuted.

M364.1.1.p: A prophecy that a saint will found a church at a certain place.

M364.2.p: A prophecy that a saint's efforts will bring about the remission of a tax.

M364.3.p: A prophecy that a saint will succeed in converting people.

M364.3.1.p: A prophecy that sinners who go to heaven will be counted by the hairs of the saint's chasuble, a priestly vestment.

M364.3.2.p: A prophecy that three great multitudes will be saved through the saint's virtue.

M364.4.p: A prophecy about the place where a saint will be resurrected.

M364.4.1.p: A prophecy that a saint will rise from the dead where a chariot breaks down.

M364.5.p: A prophecy that the region where a saint lost a tooth will be abandoned by non-Christians.

M364.6.p: A prophecy that a rainbow will appear when a saint dies.

M364.7.r: (Cf. M363.1.2.) Loomis White Magic 17; Irish myth: *Cross.
M364.7.p: A prophecy about the birth of a saint.

M364.7.1.p: Druids, pre-Christian priests, prophesy the coming of a saint.

M364.7.2.p: Non-Christians prophesy the coming of a Christian saint.

M364.7.3.p: A bishop foretells the birth of a saint.

M364.7.4.p: A prophecy that a child not yet born will become a nun, and so a saint's coming birth is foretold.

M364.8.p: A prophecy that a saint's bones will be removed from their resting place by a miracle.

M364.8.1.p: A saint predicts that his bones will be dishonored or desecrated after his death.

M364.9.p: A hero prophesies that half the churches in Ireland will be named after Saint Ciaran.

M364.10.p: A saint foresees that a church will be destroyed and later rebuilt.

M364.11.p: A saint promises that anyone buried in soil belonging to him will go to heaven.

M365.p: A prophecy that a person will have eternal peace either through an early death or through a long, troubled life.

M365.1.p: A prophecy that a hero will win fame but die young.

M365.2.p: A prophecy that a son will be brave and wise but will not stay at home, so his mother will grieve.

M365.3.p: A prophecy that a girl will be perfect in love but will die in a desert, overcome by being separated from her lover.

M366.p: A prophecy that a hero may win a lady's love but will die young; he chooses this over a long life without her.

M367.p: A prophecy that a person will be immune to certain kinds of death.

M367.1.p: A person is immune from death by wet or dry, steel or wood, sword or javelin, by day or by night, yet is killed at the edge of the sea at twilight by the sea's force and a thunderbolt.

M368.p: A prophecy that a person who misappropriates property will be punished.

M369.p: Various prophecies that do not fit the other categories.

M369.1.p: A prophecy that a person will tell three (or two) lies before dying.

M369.2.1.r: Irish myth: Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: *Thompson-Balys.
M369.2.1.p: A prophecy names a person's future husband or wife.

M369.2.1.1.p: A prophecy that a king will take a cruel stepmother back to her sons after her death is acted out before the dying queen's eyes by a family of sparrows nesting in a tree by the palace window.

M369.2.1.2.p: A prophecy that a princess will marry a bastard, that is, a man of illegitimate birth.

M369.2.2.p: A prophecy says that lovers who are not destined to be together in life will never be separated once they die.

M369.2.3.p: A prophecy foretells that a person will marry at the age of twelve.

M369.2.4.p: A prophecy says that a raja who marries a certain girl will prosper.

M369.2.5.p: A prophecy says that a descendant of a mistress will serve a descendant of a handmaid.

M369.3.p: A prophecy foretells that a certain person will fight a particular battle.

M369.4.p: The names of future kings are foretold in advance.

M369.4.1.p: A prophecy says that a bird will become king.

M369.5.p: Prophecies foretell that a land will be invaded and conquered.

M369.5.1.p: Signs that will come before the destruction of Jerusalem are foretold.

M369.6.p: The time and place where returning heroes will land are foretold in a prophecy.

M369.7.p: A prophecy is made about the birth of children.

M369.7.1.p: A prophecy foretells that twins will be born.

M369.7.2.p: A prophecy foretells the birth of an heir.

M369.7.3.p: A prophecy reveals whether an unborn child will be a boy or a girl.

M369.8.p: Prophecies are made about children who are born at the same time.

M369.9.p: A prophecy says a king will have his head pounded by a strange queen; this comes true through an unusual chain of events.

M369.10.p: A prophecy says a boy will become a great hunter.

M371.1.p: A child is exposed or killed because a parent fears that the child, prophesied to be great, will overcome the parent.

M375.3.p: A child is mutilated so that a prophecy about it will not come true.
