M376.4.p: The birth of a child destined to rule is delayed so that the prophecy about the child's reign will not come true.

M377.p: A sword that is destined to kill someone is weighted and sunk in water so that the prophecy will not come true.

M377.1.p: A stone or sword foretold to kill a certain person is ground to powder and thrown into the distant sea, or weighted and sunk, to keep the prophecy from coming true.

M381.p: A man whose death has been prophesied hides in a church, but is accidentally killed when an arrow aimed at a stag through the window strikes him instead.

M382.p: A man told by Death that he will die where he stands sells everything and moves away, but a runaway horse carries him to the very spot he feared and throws him to his death.

M390.p: A general heading for miscellaneous prophecy motifs that do not fit the more specific categories.

M391.p: A prophecy comes true exactly as foretold.

M391.1.p: A prophecy is foreseen and the attempt to prevent its fulfillment succeeds.

M391.1.1.p: A prophecy of misfortune for a prince is avoided in one respect, though not entirely.

M391.2.p: A wandering skull fulfills a prophecy, for example by bringing about the death or event it foretold.

M392.p: A queen dies of fright after hearing an evil prophecy.

M393.p: Favorable prophecies in the form of blessings or beatitudes, foretelling good fortune.

M393.1.p: A child pronounces a blessing that says each country will be filled with the things it will later be famous for.

M394.p: A prophecy announces that a hero will come.

M395.p: A prophecy says a son with a certain name will become king, so every son is given that name.

M396.p: A prophecy says two people will meet only after one of them has died.

M397.p: A prophecy says hunters will encounter a certain wild boar.

M398.p: Weather prophecies are shown to be unreliable or useless.

M400.r: *Encyc. Rel. Ethics s.v. “Cursing and Blessing”; Icelandic: *Boberg; Irish: *Cross, Beal XXI 326, 328, O’Suilleabhain 73, 88; Estonian: Loorits Grundzüge I 205ff.; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
M400.p: General heading for curses, where a person is wished harm or misfortune by someone's words.

M401.p: A contest in which two people trade curses and insults against each other in verse.

M402.p: Satire, in which a person is mocked or cursed in biting verse or speech.

M402.1.p: A woman who composes or delivers satire.

M402.1.1.p: Female satirists (women who mock others in verse or speech) are punished in hell for their satire.

M402.2.p: A satirist cannot find anyone to stand surety (vouch for him or act as guarantor) for him, as a curse or punishment for mocking others.

M403.p: A curse that makes the victim suffer constant, lasting fear.

M404.p: A curse or blessing takes effect even though the speaker did not mean it to.

M410.p: General heading for tales in which curses are uttered and pronounced against people.

M411.p: General heading for the person who utters a curse, such as a parent, beggar, god, saint, or spirit.

M411.0.1.p: A despairing person curses himself so that he and his palace sink into the earth.

M411.1.r: Penzer IV 230 n. 2; Irish myth: *Cross; Lithuanian: Balys Index No. 3591; Spanish Exempla: Keller; Greek: Fox 50 (Oedipus), Grote I 247; India: Thompson-Balys.
M411.1.p: A parent utters a curse against a child.

M411.1.1.r: (Cf. S31.) Icelandic: *Boberg; Modern Icelandic: Rittershaus 34, 48, 50, 58, 66, 161, Sveinsson FFC LXXXIII xxviii ff.
M411.1.1.p: A stepmother utters a curse, often against her stepchild.

M411.1.2.p: A foster mother utters a curse against a child in her care.

M411.2.r: “May your bread turn to stones!” *Kittredge Witchcraft 132, 452 n. 52; England: Baughman; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 183; India: *Thompson-Balys.
M411.2.p: A beggar who is refused what he asks for curses the person who turned him away.

M411.3.p: A dying man utters a curse as he dies.

M411.4.r: Irish: MacCulloch Celtic 74ff., *Cross; Greek: Grote I 147; India: *Thompson-Balys.
M411.4.p: A man is pursued by the hatred of the gods, who curse him.

M411.4.1.p: A god utters a curse against a person.

M411.5.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg; Spanish: Espinosa Jr. No. 106; Italian: Basile Pentamerone
M411.5.p: An old woman utters a curse, in a satirical manner.

M411.6.p: A druid (a priest of the ancient Celtic religion) utters a curse.

M411.6.1.p: A druid's curse makes the land barren so that nothing will grow in it.

M411.7.p: A spirit utters a curse against a person.

M411.8.r: *Loomis White Magic 100f.; Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: *Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
M411.8.p: A saint or prophet utters a curse against someone.

M411.8.1.p: A saint curses an offender by ringing bells against him.

M411.8.2.p: A hermit (a holy man living alone) curses men who have killed his pet bear, and all of those men die.

M411.8.3.p: A saint places a curse on certain places because someone gave him an offensive answer.

M411.8.4.p: A saint lays a curse on certain animals.

M411.8.5.p: A saint curses books that an inhospitable host has hidden, so that no one may ever read them.

M411.9.p: A giantess lays a curse on whoever on earth eventually hears her.

M411.10.p: A berserk (wildly raging) giant or ogre lays a curse on someone.

M411.11.p: A girl lays a curse on someone in revenge for the murder of her foster father.

M411.11.1.p: A female warrior (an amazon, called skjaldmær in Old Norse) lays a curse on someone.

M411.12.p: A witch lays a curse on someone.

M411.13.p: A thrall (an enslaved person or bondservant) lays a curse on someone.

M411.14.p: A priest lays a curse on someone.

M411.14.1.p: A priest curses a sinner so that not even his grave will be at rest.

M411.14.2.p: An anchorite (a hermit who has withdrawn from the world) lays a curse on someone.

M411.14.3.p: A Brahmin (a member of the Hindu priestly class) lays a curse on someone.

M411.15.p: A monk lays a curse on someone.

M411.16.p: A fairy lays a curse on a village.

M411.17.p: A king lays a curse on someone.

M411.18.p: A poet lays a curse on someone.

M411.19.p: An animal lays a curse on someone.

M411.19.1.p: A wounded animal lays a curse on someone.

M411.19.2.p: An ox curses a man who has been ungrateful to it, so that the curse takes effect on him.

M411.20.p: A curse is uttered by a man's or woman's spouse, and it takes effect on the person it is aimed at.

M411.21.p: A god or other divine being in disguise pronounces a curse on someone.

M411.22.p: The head of a religious order, such as an abbot or bishop, pronounces a curse.

M411.23.p: A person who has been wronged by someone pronounces a curse on the wrongdoer.

M411.24.p: A wise man or sage places a curse on a city.

M412.p: Concerns the time at which a curse is pronounced.

M412.1.r: *Type 410; *BP I 434; Köhler-Bolte Zs. f. Vksk. VI 70 (to Gonzenbach No. 28); Irish myth: Cross; Icelandic: *Boberg.
M412.1.p: A curse is pronounced over a child at the moment of its birth.

M412.2.p: A curse is pronounced on the wedding night of a couple.

M413.p: Concerns the place from which a curse is pronounced.

M413.1.r: Irish: Plummer clxxiv, Cross; Italian Novella: Rotunda.
M413.1.p: A curse is pronounced from a high place, and it falls with full force on whatever it is aimed at.

M414.p: Concerns who or what is the target of a curse.

M414.1.p: A god is the one who is cursed.

M414.2.p: A goddess is the one who is cursed.

M414.3.p: A saint is the one who is cursed.

M414.4.p: A four-year-old girl is the one who is cursed.

M414.5.p: A king is the one who is cursed.

M414.6.p: A poet is the one who is cursed.

M414.7.p: Hostages are the ones who are cursed.

M414.8.p: Animals are the ones who are cursed.

M414.8.1.p: A curse is pronounced that turns mice (or rats or cats) into a punishment or affliction.

M414.8.2.p: A curse is laid on pigs, placing them under a misfortune or punishment.

M414.8.3.p: A curse is laid on a serpent, condemning it to a punishment or affliction.

M414.8.4.p: A curse is laid on birds, placing them under a misfortune or punishment.

M414.9.p: A curse is laid on a wife's lover, bringing misfortune on the man who has taken up with her.

M414.10.p: A thief is put under a curse as punishment for stealing.

M414.11.p: A man who reveals secrets is put under a curse as punishment for his betrayal.

M414.12.p: The earth itself is put under a curse.

M414.13.p: A god is put under a curse, forcing the deity into some misfortune or punishment.

M414.13.1.p: A god is cursed to live the life of a cat for twelve full years in the house of a huntsman on earth.

M415.r: Penzer VI 103 n. 1, 162 n. 1; Irish myth: Cross; India: Thompson-Balys.
M415.p: A curse is pronounced that cannot be taken back or undone once spoken.

M416.p: A gift or good wish is spoiled by a curse attached to it, so that the blessing turns into a burden or punishment. In the Norse example, Odin gives a man threefold life and Thor ordains that he will commit a crime in each life; Odin gives him the best weapons while Thor denies him land and other goods.

M416.1.p: A curse is attached to a gift of great strength: the recipient is cursed with the appetite of twelve men.

M416.2.p: A curse grants eternal life but without eternal youth, so the person lives on forever while growing old.

M418.p: Describes the ways or methods by which a curse is pronounced or carried out.

M418.1.p: A curse is worked by building a fire of stones in the fireplace, and whoever later removes the stones is cursed.

M420.p: Ways in which a person can survive or get free from a curse once it has been laid on them.

M421.p: A curse ends when a child is born to the cursed person.

M422.r: Irish: Plummer clxxiii, *Cross, Beal XXI 326, O’Suilleabhain 73.
M422.p: A curse is passed on from the one who suffers it to another person or thing, freeing the original victim.

M423.p: A curse is lifted when those under it reform and mend their ways.

M425.p: A curse is turned by God into a blessing instead of harm.

M427.p: A curse falls on everyone on earth who hears trolls' names spoken so that they die, but a person hiding in a cave escapes it because he is inside the earth.

M428.p: A curse is lessened by a god once the cursed person performs an superhuman task.

M429.p: A collection of assorted ways a curse can be lifted or overcome.

M429.1.p: A curse is lifted by burning someone's vomit.

M429.2.p: A curse is lifted by putting pins around a horse's heart and then boiling it.

M429.3.p: A curse is lifted by burning an animal in a pile of straw.

M429.4.p: A curse is lifted by heating the colter (the blade at the front of a plow) in the stove.

M429.5.p: A curse is lifted by pricking a louse and hanging it on the wall.

M429.6.p: A curse is lifted by dropping a five-cent coin into the churn.

M429.7.p: A curse is lifted by putting a piece of silver into a gun.

M430.p: A general heading for curses that are laid on particular people.

M431.p: A general heading for curses that cause bodily injury to the person cursed.

M431.1.r: *Type 1331; *BP II 219 n. 1; Irish myth: *Cross; and notes to J2074.
M431.1.p: A curse causes the cursed person to lose an eye.

M431.2.p: A curse makes toads come out of the cursed person's mouth.

M431.3.p: A curse makes fire burn the cursed person's hands and feet.

M431.4.p: A curse causes the cursed person's arm to fall off.

M431.4.1.p: A curse causes the cursed person's hand to drop off.

M431.5.p: A curse keeps a wound from healing.

M431.6.p: A wicked stepmother is cursed so that fire is lit under her.

M431.7.r: India: Thompson-Balys; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera II 1050.
M431.7.p: A curse that causes the person to be afflicted with leprosy, a disfiguring skin and nerve disease.

M431.8.p: A curse that makes the wife of an enemy unable to bear children.

M431.9.p: A curse that causes the person's head to split into seven pieces.

M431.10.p: A curse that condemns the person to be tormented by bad dreams every night.

M432.r: Pauli (ed. Bolte) No. 456; Hdwb. d. Märchens I 547a nn. 127—139.
M432.p: A curse that dooms the person to be carried away by an evil spirit.

M433.p: Endymion, a figure of classical myth, is given an endless sleep as a punishment or gift.

M434.p: A curse that causes the person to be swallowed by a siren, a sea creature or enchantress who lures and devours.

M435.p: A curse that prevents the person from eating food from his own table, because whatever he tries to eat is snatched away by harpies, winged monsters.

M436.p: A curse that makes a prince fall in love with the daughter of a witch.

M437.p: A curse that causes a woman to give birth to a monstrous, deformed child.

M437.1.p: A curse in the form of a saying, "What I carry may you carry; what you carry may I carry," which here is laid on an ungrateful pregnant woman by a cat, so that she bears cats and the cat bears twin girls.

M437.2.p: Jealous sisters lay a curse, through the god Thor, on one of them's child so that it will never grow or thrive.

M438.p: A curse that brings humiliation or disgrace upon the person.

M438.1.p: A curse that forces a man, specifically a poet, to kiss a leper.

M438.2.p: A curse that makes the hero unable to bear the sight of blood.

M438.3.p: A girl is bewitched so that no man will stay faithful to her.

M438.4.p: A curse that keeps the hero in a state like death until the person who cursed him dies.

M438.5.p: A dying father condemns his weak son to serve his brothers as a servant.

M441.p: A curse that makes everything the person attempts end in failure.

M441.1.p: A curse that makes a man's sword fail him when he is in danger.

M441.1.1.p: A curse says that when a man's brothers' swords bite the very best, a single man will kill them all. The curse means the swords of the brothers will fail them in danger, so they will die at one man's hand.

M442.p: A curse that makes the person, or the person's descendants, physically deformed or misshapen.

M442.1.p: A curse that the person's descendants will be ill-formed or unsightly in body.

M442.2.p: A curse that a she-wolf will carry off a man's genitals.

M443.p: A curse that brings poverty and want on the person.

M443.1.p: A curse that the person will lack food, shelter, and good company.

M444.p: A curse that the person will have no children.

M444.1.p: A curse laid on an unborn child, so that the child is born dead.

M445.p: A giant is cursed so that neither heaven nor earth will take him in, leaving him with no resting place in either world.

M446.p: A curse that forces the person to undertake a dangerous quest or journey.

M446.1.p: A curse that forces the person to undertake a dangerous revenge for his father.

M448.r: Tupper and Ogle Walter Map 91; India: Thompson-Balys; Eskimo (Central Eskimo): Boas RBAE VI 585.
M448.p: A curse that makes the person sink into the earth.

M448.1.p: A curse that the ground will swallow the person's children.

M451.r: England, U.S.: *Baughman; Jewish: Neuman; Chinese: Eberhard FFC CXX 126.
M451.p: A curse that brings death on the person.

M451.1.p: A curse that the person will die by suicide.

M451.2.p: A curse that the person will die by drowning.

M452.p: A curse that makes the person insane.

M453.p: A curse that after the person dies, the corpse must be put in three different places.

M454.p: A curse that changes the person's sex, turning a man into a woman or a woman into a man.

M455.r: (Cf. K1837.4.) Irish myth: *Cross; Icelandic: Lagerholm lxi—ii.
M455.p: A curse that leaves the person unable to rest, restless and constantly moving.

M455.1.p: A hero is cursed so that he cannot stay still and must keep wandering, except while on a boat or in a tent, until he sees a certain girl.

M455.2.p: A curse makes a person unable to stay in love with the same woman for more than twelve months.

M455.3.p: A servant or slave is cursed to sit on a chest, yelling, and never be allowed any rest.

M455.4.p: A couple is cursed to wander until someone points out the new home where their race is to settle.

M458.p: A person is cursed to be turned into stone.

M459.p: A general heading for curses on individual persons that do not fit the more specific categories.

M459.1.p: A curse makes a woman unable or unwilling to travel far from home.

M460.r: Irish: Plummer clxxiv, *Cross; England, Wales, U.S.: Baughman; Icelandic: *Boberg; Greek: Fox 120 (Tantalus), Grote I 244f. (Oedipus); Jewish: Neuman; Buddhist myth: Malalasekera I 108.
M460.p: A general heading for curses that fall on whole families or lines of descent.

M460.1.p: A curse on a family makes its children fall sick.

M461.p: A curse says that the descendants of nine robbers may never grow beyond nine in number.

M461.1.p: A curse on a village says its descendants may never exceed a certain number.

M462.p: A curse says that a people or dynasty will lose its power to rule.

M463.r: Irish myth: *Cross; Jewish: Neuman; India: Thompson-Balys.
M463.p: A curse falls on an entire tribe or district.

M464.p: A woman places a curse on her own caste or social group, that they should remain naked and uneducated.

M470.p: A general heading for curses placed on objects or animals.

M471.p: A general heading for curses placed on animals.

M471.1.p: A curse makes a cow give red milk.

M471.1.1.p: A curse makes a cow's milk refuse to turn into butter.

M471.2.r: Irish myth: Cross; French Canadian: Sister Marie Ursule.
M471.2.p: A curse is laid on pigs so that they grow lean and thin.

M471.3.p: A curse says that a person's horses will die.

M471.3.1.p: A curse that makes a horse go lame, so that it can no longer walk or run properly.

M474.p: A curse placed on a piece of land, so that the land is damaged or made barren.

M475.p: A curse placed on a city, bringing it some misfortune.

M475.1.p: A curse that keeps a city from ever growing larger or prospering.

M476.p: A curse placed on a river.

M476.1.p: A curse on a river or sea that leaves no fish in it from that day on.

M477.p: A curse placed on a lake.

M477.1.p: A curse on a lake under which fire comes out of the water and sets the surrounding forest ablaze.

M490.p: A general heading for curses that do not fit the more specific categories listed under it.

M491.p: The mere presence of a person under a curse brings disaster to the land where they are.

M493.p: Someone cursed by demons is blessed instead, and someone blessed by demons is cursed.
